subject: religious-studies
title: Analogy, Symbol and Language Games
welcome_lead: Survey three theological models of how religious language signifies: Aquinas's analogy, Tillich's symbol, and Wittgenstein's language games.
meta_desc: A-Level OCR Religious Studies adventure on Aquinas on analogy, Tillich on symbol, and Wittgenstein/Phillips on language games.
final_note: You have weighed three models of religious meaning and the critiques they face.

concepts.def: Used in the same sense in two contexts.
An attribute applies properly to one being and derivatively to another.
An attribute applies to each being in proportion to the kind of being it is.
For Tillich, a sign that participates in the reality to which it points.
Wittgenstein's rule-governed linguistic practice embedded in a form of life.

walkthroughs.body_html: Summa Theologiae I, Q.13 treats divine names. Univocal predication makes God a creature; equivocal predication makes theology unintelligible. Analogy steers between. By attribution, 'healthy' applies properly to the body and derivatively to the medicine; so 'good' applies properly to God and derivatively to creatures. By proportion, each thing is good in the mode of its own being.

Paul Tillich's Dynamics of Faith (1957) distinguishes sign from symbol. A traffic sign points away from itself; a flag participates in the country it symbolises. Religious symbols open levels of reality otherwise closed. They are born, grow and die. The only non-symbolic statement we can make about God is that God is Being-Itself; all else is symbolic.

Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations (1953) breaks with the picture theory of language: meaning is use within a language game, embedded in a form of life. D. Z. Phillips applied this to religion: the believer's 'God exists' is not a quasi-scientific hypothesis but a move in a distinctive language game. Critics charge fideism, isolating religious language from rational assessment.
